#### Fudan NLP Lab 2026-1-21 ### **Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize?** **Evaluating the Synthesis Gap with Expert Taxonomies** **Ming Zhang** [†*] **, Jiabao Zhuang** [*] **, Wenqing Jing** [*] **, Ziyu Kong, Jingyi Deng,** Yujiong Shen, Kexin Tan, Yuhang Zhao, Ning Luo, Renzhe Zheng, Jiahui Lin, Mingqi Wu, Long Ma, Yi Zou, Shihan Dou, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang [†], Xuanjing Huang Fudan NLP Group ``` mingzhang23@m.fudan.edu.cn, qz@fudan.edu.cn ``` **Deep Research Agents are increasingly used for automated survey generation. However, whether** **they can write surveys like human experts remains unclear. Existing benchmarks focus on fluency** **or citation accuracy, but none evaluates the core capabilities: retrieving essential papers and or-** **ganizing them into coherent knowledge structures. We introduce TaxoBench, a diagnostic bench-** **mark derived from 72 highly-cited computer science surveys. We manually extract expert-authored** **taxonomy trees containing 3,815 precisely categorized citations as ground truth. Our benchmark** **supports two evaluation modes: Deep Research mode tests end-to-end retrieval and organization** **given only a topic, while Bottom-Up mode isolates structuring capability by providing the exact** **papers human experts used. We evaluate 7 leading Deep Research agents and 12 frontier LLMs.** **Results reveal a dual bottleneck: the best agent recalls only 20.9% of expert-selected papers, and** **even with perfect input, the best model achieves only 0.31 ARI in organization. Current deep re-** **search agents remain far from expert-level survey writing. Our benchmark is publicly available at** **`[https://github.com/KongLongGeFDU/TaxoBench](https://github.com/KongLongGeFDU/TaxoBench)`** **.** #### **1. Introduction** Large Language Models (LLMs) have ex panded from basic assistance to complex cog nitive tasks in scientific workflows, includ ing automatic academic writing (Liang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025), peer review assis tance (Liang et al., 2024; Thakkar et al., 2025), and scientific discovery acceleration (Jablonka et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2025). As academic literature grows exponentially, Deep Research Agents (Schmidgall et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) have emerged as promising tools for au tomated survey generation (de la Torre-López et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Yan et al., 2025). However, a fundamental question re mains: **Can these agents write surveys like** **human experts?** Consider how domain experts write sur veys. They do not begin with a fixed outline *Equal Contribution. †Corresponding Author. Survey Topic: Aligning LLMs with Human ...... Agent **Figure 1** | **Deep Research Agents** for survey generation. Given a survey topic, the agent au tonomously conducts web-based research to re trieve relevant papers and organizes them into a hierarchical taxonomy. Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? Evaluating the Synthesis Gap with Expert Taxonomies When Recall high enough, can Agents generate Taxonomy matching Ground Truth? **Figure 2** | Overview of TaxoBench, (1) **Deep Research Mode** targets end-to-end retrieval and taxon omy generation ( _𝑇_ [ˆ] ) from a query. (2) **Bottom-Up Mode** isolates organization logic, reconstructing hierarchies ( _𝑇_ [∗] ) from fixed papers using varying input granularities and (3) **Data Example** illustrates the dataset structure, detailing the ground truth JSON schema and taxonomy mapping. and search for papers to fill it. Instead, they follow a bottom-up process: reading hundreds of pa pers, identifying seminal work, and gradually organizing knowledge into a coherent taxonomy that reveals the field’s intellectual structure (Wang et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2023). This taxonomy re flects a deep understanding of how ideas relate to each other. Existing benchmarks fail to evaluate this cognitive process. Current evaluations focus on sur face metrics such as fluency or citation accuracy (Eldifrawi et al., 2024; Wadden et al., 2020), not whether agents can replicate how experts actually write surveys. We decompose this question into two challenges: **Challenge 1: Can Deep Research agents identify the papers experts would select?** A survey is defined by what it includes. Human experts develop judgment for which papers are foundational and which can be omitted. Current evaluations rarely measure whether agents share this judgment. **Challenge 2: Can Deep Research agents organize papers as experts would?** A survey taxon omy is not arbitrary clustering. It reflects how concepts, methods, and applications relate hierarchi cally. No existing benchmark evaluates whether agents can produce expert-like organization. To address these challenges, we introduce TaxoBench, the first benchmark to evaluate whether Deep Research Agents can write academic surveys like human experts. We collect 72 highly-cited surveys from authoritative computer science venues, covering subfields including multimodal learn ing, reinforcement learning, and alignment. From each survey, we manually extract the taxonomy tree representing how experts organized the field. This yields 3,815 precisely categorized citations as ground truth. We describe the construction pipeline in Section 2. Our benchmark supports two evaluation modes. **Deep Research mode** requires agents to retrieve and organize papers given only a topic, testing end-to-end capability. **Bottom-Up mode** provides the exact papers experts used, isolating organization capability from retrieval. Within Bottom-Up mode, we vary input granularity by providing abstracts, summaries, or extracted contributions to examine 2 Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? Evaluating the Synthesis Gap with Expert Taxonomies what information enables expert-like organization. We evaluate 7 Deep Research agents and 12 frontier LLMs, revealing a **dual bottleneck** in re trieval and organization. First, retrieval fails: even the best agent recalls only 20.9% of expert selected papers, with most below 5%. Second, organization struggles: given perfect input, the best model achieves only 0.31 ARI. Retrieval also predicts structure quality (Spearman _𝜌_ =0.83), confirm ing these failures compound. Current agents remain far from human-level survey writing. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We release TaxoBench, the first benchmark to evaluate survey writing from a human cognition perspective, featuring 72 expert-authored taxonomy trees and 3,815 categorized citations. 2. We carefully design a dual-layer evaluation framework with tailored metrics covering retrieval and organization, along with controlled experiments on input granularity. 3. We evaluate 7 Deep Research agents and 12 frontier LLMs, revealing fundamental gaps and releasing all data and code publicly. #### **2. TaxoBench** We introduce TaxoBench, a benchmark to evaluate whether Deep Research Agents can write surveys like human experts. This section describes our data construction pipeline. **2.1. Task Definition** When human experts write a survey, they produce a taxonomy that organizes the literature into a coherent knowledge structure. We formalize this as the core evaluation task: given a research topic, can agents produce a taxonomy that matches expert organization? A taxonomy tree _𝑇_ = ( _𝑉, 𝐸_ ) consists of nodes _𝑉_ representing concepts or topics, and edges _𝐸_ representing hierarchical relationships. Leaf nodes correspond to individual papers, while internal nodes represent conceptual categories. The ground truth taxonomy _𝑇_ [∗] is extracted from expert authored surveys, capturing how domain experts organize knowledge after extensive reading. **2.2. Survey Collection** We collect surveys from authoritative computer science venues, focusing on LLM-related research. Our collection covers diverse subfields including multimodal learning, reinforcement learning, align ment, and agents. To ensure quality, we apply two filters: - Surveys must contain explicit taxonomy figures, identified by querying captions for terms such as “taxonomy” or “typology.” - Surveys must be highly cited, ensuring alignment with expert consensus. This process yields 72 high-quality surveys spanning 8 research domains. **2.3. Taxonomy Extraction** From each survey, we manually extract the taxonomy tree that organizes the surveyed literature. We employ human annotation rather than automated extraction for three reasons: (1) taxonomy figures 3 Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? All annotators hold Ph.D. degrees in computer science, ensuring domain expertise for accurate in terpretation of survey content. Annotators identify the hierarchical structure from taxonomy figures and map cited papers to corresponding leaf nodes using the original text, diagrams, and bibliogra phies. We represent each taxonomy as a directory structure: topics become folders, subtopics become subfolders, and papers become text files. This format naturally preserves hierarchical relationships and enables efficient processing. The annotation process includes three quality controls: - **Disambiguation** : Resolving papers cited under multiple names or versions. - **Deduplication** : Merging duplicate entries across survey sections. - **Validation** : Cross-checking node assignments against survey text. **2.4. Dataset Statistics** Table 1 summarizes key statistics. We collect 72 surveys with an average of 354.5 citations per survey, confirming their high impact and expert recognition. From these surveys, we extract taxonomy trees covering 3,815 papers in total. On average, each taxonomy organizes 53 papers across 3.2 hierarchy levels with 12.4 leaf categories. Figure 2 (3) shows example taxonomies from our dataset. The diversity of tree structures, domain coverage, and organization styles provides a challenging testbed. Unlike synthetic benchmarks, our ground truth captures authentic expert cognition, namely the knowledge structures that emerge from months of reading and synthesis. #### **3. Evaluation Framework** We design a dual-layer evaluation framework to assess whether models can construct taxonomy trees like human experts. Following the notation in Section 2, let _𝑇_ [∗] = ( _𝑉_ [∗] _, 𝐸_ [∗] ) denote the ground truth taxonomy from expert surveys, and _𝑇_ [ˆ] = ( _𝑉,_ [ˆ] _𝐸_ [ˆ] ) denote the model-generated taxonomy. We evaluate at two levels: **Leaf-Level** (paper assignment quality) and **Hierarchy-Level** (structural organization quality), using six metrics tailored to our two evaluation modes. 4 Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? For further details, please refer to the Appendix D. #### **4. Benchmarking LLMs on TaxoBench** We evaluate 7 leading Deep Research agents and 12 frontier LLMs on TaxoBench. This section describes our experimental setup and presents key findings. **Deep Research Mode.** We evaluate Deep Research agents in their standard usage: given only a survey topic, agents must independently retrieve papers and organize them into a taxonomy. We test 7 agents: o3, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Doubao. This mode assesses end-to-end survey-writing capability. **Bottom-Up Mode.** We evaluate frontier LLMs on pure organization capability by providing the exact papers from expert taxonomies _𝑇_ [∗] . This eliminates retrieval as a variable, directly testing whether models can structure knowledge like experts. We test 12 models including Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT 5, Gemini-3-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-Max, and Kimi-K2, each with both standard and thinking variants. 6 Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? Table 3 shows the impact of input granularity on organization quality. Coun terintuitively, adding richer information (summaries or core-task & contributions) does not improve, and often degrades, alignment with expert classifications. As shown in Figure 7, for Claude-4.5-Sonnet, ARI drops from 0.27 (Title+Abstract) to 0.24 (+Summary), yet Soft F1 improves from 0.86 to 0.88 and LLM-judge score rises from 2.53 to 2.59. These results reveal a critical insight: additional information helps models generate taxonomies that _appear_ more reasonable, but these structures diverge further from expert classification bound aries. Models leverage richer semantics to construct their own organizational logic rather than learn ing expert conventions. This suggests that the gap between model and expert cognition lies not in information access, but in implicit domain knowledge that text comprehension cannot capture. #### **5. Related Work** **5.1. Deep Research-aided Survey Generation** As academic literature grows exponentially, automated survey generation has become a prominent research area. With the advancement of deep research agents (Google, 2025c; Li et al., 2025b; Ope nAI, 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025), recent studies have also explored leveraging LLMs for end-to-end survey generation (Lahiri et al., 2025). Most approaches adopt a structure-then-content mode: Auto Survey (Wang et al., 2024b) employs a two-stage generation approach, prior work (Hu et al., 2024) 10 Can Deep Research Agents Find and Organize? Evaluating the Synthesis Gap with Expert Taxonomies uses citation networks to construct taxonomy trees, and SurveyForge (Yan et al., 2025) integrates human-curated outlines with literature retrieval. These methods share a common assumption: that LLMs can inherently organize papers into co herent knowledge structures. However, no prior work directly evaluates this capability. Our bench mark fills this gap by measuring whether models can reproduce expert-level knowledge organization. **5.2. Deep Research Evaluation** Existing evaluation frameworks focus on different capabilities: multi-hop retrieval and reasoning (Ai ling et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), web-based retrieval (Deng et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025), and automated report generation (Du et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). However, none assesses the core ability to retrieve and organize knowledge structures. Although recent works (Sun et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025) include outline evaluation, they rely on LLM-as a-judge without validation against human consensus. In contrast, TaxoBench uses expert-authored taxonomies from published surveys as ground truth, providing direct measurement of alignment with human expert cognition. #### **6. Conclusion** We introduce TaxoBench, the first benchmark to evaluate whether Deep Research Agents can write surveys like human experts, featuring 72 expert-authored taxonomy trees with 3,815 categorized citations as ground truth. Our evaluation of 7 Deep Research agents and 12 frontier LLMs reveals a dual bottleneck: retrieval fails (best agent: 20.9% recall, most below 5%) and organization struggles (best model: 0.31 ARI even with perfect input). Retrieval quality predicts structural quality (Spearman _𝜌_ =0.83), yet richer input improves plausibility without improving expert alignment. These findings show current agents remain far from human-level survey writing. The gap lies in implicit domain knowledge that text comprehension cannot capture. We hope TaxoBench could support future research on closing this gap. #### **Limitations** While TaxoBench establishes a rigorous framework for assessing knowledge structuring in Deep Research, we aim to extend it to further enhance its generalizability. Currently, our evaluation prioritizes frontier closed-source LLMs to establish a robust and representative baseline. Moving forward, we plan to extend this benchmark to a broader spectrum of open-source models to quan tify performance disparities across diverse architectures, thereby fostering advancements within the open-source community. #### **References** Yu Ai-ling, Yao Lan, Ailing Yu, Liu Jing-nan, Lan Yao, Chen Zhe, Jingnan Liu, Yin Jiajun, Zhe Chen, Wang Yuan, Jiajun Yin, Liao Xinhao, Yuan Wang, Zhiling Ye, Xinhao Liao, Li Ji, Zhiling Ye, Yue Yun, Ji Li, Yun Yue, Zhou Hualei, Hansong Xiao, Guo Chun-xiao, Hualei Zhou, Wei Peng, Chunxiao Guo, Liu Junwei, Peng Wei, Jinjie Gu, Junwei Liu, and Jinjie Gu. Additional dataset information** **Human Annotator Information.** The data construction process for this study involved manual an notation conducted entirely by a recruited team. All annotators are recruited experts holding Ph.D. degrees in Computer Science and possess extensive professional expertise in academic writing and literature analysis. The primary annotation tasks encompassed: (1) systematically collecting survey papers related to Large Language Models (LLMs) from authoritative computer science conferences and journals; (2) filtering for papers containing explicit knowledge structures using heuristic rules (e.g., querying figure captions for terms such as “taxonomy” or “typology”); (3) selecting candidate papers based on citation counts to ensure alignment with high-impact expert consensus; and (4) precisely extracting hierarchical classification structures and mapping cited papers to corresponding leaf nodes based on the full text, figures, and references, ultimately constructing an unambiguous directory structure. **Data Consent and Copyright.** All data utilized in this study are derived from publicly available academic literature hosted on open-access repositories (e.g., arXiv) or made available through the open-access policies of academic publishers. Second, during the evaluation phase, we utilized only text segments containing scientific content (e.g., titles and abstracts). Finally, as the primary objective of this re search is to evaluate the retrieval and knowledge organization capabilities of Artificial Intelligence, it does not involve human subject experimentation. List of Evaluation Models** In this study, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the retrieval and knowledge organiza tion capabilities of seven Deep Research Agents and twelve state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs). The evaluated models are detailed below. _**Deep Research Agents**_ - **o3** (El-Kishky et al., 2025): OpenAI’s deep research model is an agent designed specifically for complex analysis and research tasks. By integrating diverse data sources—including web search, remote MCP servers, and internal vector stores, it executes multi-step autonomous research to generate comprehensive reports suitable for legal analysis, market research, and scientific literature reviews. - **Doubao Deep Research** (ByteDance, 2025): By deeply integrating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) with search engines, this model enables dynamic, multi-turn interactions involving search and tool invocation during reasoning, thereby significantly enhancing problem-solving capabilities and information accuracy in complex tasks. - **DeepSeek Search** (DeepSeek, 2025): This model’s web search capability is implemented via API-configured browser plugins, allowing it to dynamically retrieve and integrate the latest web information during response generation. - **Gemini Deep Research** (Google, 2025b): An autonomous research assistant capable of inte grating public web information with private workspace data. It employs multi-step planning, search, and reasoning to generate comprehensive reports featuring detailed thought processes and interactive content. - **Grok DeepSearch** (xAI, 2025): A research tool focused on high-speed response and real-time information integration. It rapidly scans public platform content to generate concise, multi source reports within minutes. - **Perplexity Deep Research** (Perplexity, 2025): A professional-grade deep research tool charac terized by high accessibility and leading benchmark performance. It automates the generation of detailed analysis reports through iterative search and reasoning. - **Qwen-Deep-Research** (Alibaba, 2025): A model featuring automatic research planning and multi-turn iterative search. It employs a distinctive two-stage workflow: first clarifying the research scope via follow-up confirmation questions, and subsequently executing the full re search task. _**Bottom-up Models**_ - **Claude-4.5-Sonnet** (Anthropic, 2025): A world-leading model specializing in coding, com plex agent construction, and computer-use tasks, demonstrating significant advancements in reasoning and mathematics. We use the Claude-4.5-Sonnet-0929 version in our experiments. - **Claude-4.5-Sonnet (Thinking)** (Anthropic, 2025): The extended thinking mode of Claude 4.5-Sonnet.
